tier_reason: First-party go test -bench output in graphemes/README.md and words/README.md, with public harnesses graphemes/comparative/comparative_test.go (rivo/uniseg v0.4.7 pinned) and words/comparative/comparative_test.go (blevesearch/segment v0.9.1), on an Apple M2; the Go toolchain version is never printed and the results are single runs, so not A, and no independent measurement exists, so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Graphemes (graphemes/README.md, Apple M2): mixed multilingual sample 142635 ns/op, 245.12 MB/s versus rivo/uniseg 2018284 ns/op, 17.32 MB/s (about 14.2x, derived from page data); ASCII 8846 ns/op, 508.73 MB/s versus 366760 ns/op, 12.27 MB/s (about 41.5x, derived from page data); 0 allocs/op for both. The uniseg side uses uniseg.NewGraphemes/Graphemes.Next, which calls StepString and computes word, sentence and line-break boundaries plus monospace width on every step, while uax29 computes grapheme boundaries only, so these ratios overstate a graphemes-only comparison (uniseg's lighter FirstGraphemeClusterInString API was not benchmarked). Words (words/README.md): multilingual 164760 ns/op, 212.20 MB/s versus blevesearch/segment 593147 ns/op, 58.94 MB/s (about 3.6x, derived from page data); ASCII prose 224518 ns/op, 282.38 MB/s versus 1387461 ns/op, 45.69 MB/s (about 6.2x, derived from page data); the blevesearch loop also copies the input string to []byte on every iteration (40960 and 65537 B/op, 1 alloc/op).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain version not printed in either README output; graphemes/comparative/go.mod declares go 1.24.2 and words/comparative/go.mod declares go 1.18; plain go test -bench defaults, no flags stated
corrections.caveats: Author-run, single runs without variance, on one Apple M2 (darwin/arm64, -8 suffix so GOMAXPROCS 8); Go version not stated, so not tier A even though the harnesses are public and trivial to rerun. Not like-for-like on work done: rivo/uniseg's Graphemes.Next (v0.4.7) runs StepString, which also computes word, sentence and line-break boundaries and monospace width per cluster, so the 14.2x and 41.5x grapheme ratios partly measure that extra work; uniseg's graphemes-only FirstGraphemeClusterInString was not compared. Unicode versions differ: uax29 implements Unicode 17 (trie generated from the 17.0.0 UCD, GB9c Indic conjunct rule implemented) while uniseg v0.4.7 implements Unicode 15.0.0 without GB9c, and the 34,962-byte multilingual sample has about 2,000 Indic code points, so boundaries can differ there (extra work on the uax29 side). The ASCII fast path (any ASCII byte other than CR followed by an ASCII byte or end of input is a single grapheme) is correct under UAX #29 (no ASCII Extend, SpacingMark, Prepend or RI; CR LF handled by the slow path), and the ASCII input is a 4,500-byte repeated pangram that hits it on almost every byte. For words, the harness itself notes word counts may differ from blevesearch/segment because of different rule implementations, and the blevesearch loop pays a string-to-[]byte copy per iteration. Baselines are Go libraries only: no ICU, simdutf, C or golang.org/x/text comparison. Conformance is checked against the official Unicode test suites in CI.

notes: Numbers on both README pages match the record exactly and the derived ratios check out (bytes per op are consistent across rows: 34,962 for the sample, 4,500 for the ASCII string). Tier C stands; the main new shortcoming is that the uniseg baseline call does grapheme plus word, sentence, line and width work, so the grapheme ratios are inflated. License MIT, 123 stars, 7 forks, last commit 2026-02-16, not archived or a fork, all confirmed.

tier_reason: HandBrake issue 839 (opened by CvH, 2017-07-26) gives 'NLMeans ~17-20fps with KNLMeansCL 50-55fps' encode speed with no hardware, resolution, settings or versions, so these are numbers without methodology; the project's wiki Benchmark page states full hardware but has no baseline column.

corrections.caveats: The only head-to-head number is a 2017 user anecdote in a HandBrake feature-request issue (CvH, issue closed): no GPU or CPU model, resolution, filter settings, versions or compiler stated. The figures are whole-encode fps (encoder included), not filter-only throughput, and compare an OpenCL GPU filter against HandBrake's CPU NLMeans with denoise strength not matched, so the 2.5-3.2x is a rough system-level indication. The baseline is HandBrake's own NLMeans port, not an FFmpeg component or other category incumbent. The project's wiki Benchmark page lists absolute fps only, with no baseline: 1920x1080, KNLMeansCL(d=1, a=2, s=4, device_type='GPU'), version 1.0.2, Intel Core i5-4690 3.9 GHz, 8 GB DDR3-1600, AMD Radeon RX 480, Windows 10 64-bit; GRAY int8 25 fps down to 9 fps for single-precision 4:4:4 and RGB. Search snippets of the Doom9 thread (forum blocked, snippet only) say TNLMeans was about equal or slightly ahead on a weak CPU (C2D 4400) and that a GPU TNLMeans variant reached about 30 fps against 25 fps for KNLMeansCL in one user's test, so the advantage depends on hardware and settings. No FFmpeg nlmeans or nlmeans_opencl comparison with numbers was found (FastFlix issue 202 only says nlmeans_opencl is 'way faster' than the CPU filter). Last commit 2023-01-05 (merge of pinterf pull request #53); pinterf's fork carries later work. Repository page showed 572 commits.

notes: Issue 839 quote, date and author match the record; derived 2.5-3.2x is correct (50/20 and 55/17). License GPL-3.0 confirmed from the LICENSE file; 113 stars, 30 forks, not archived or a fork; last commit 2023-01-05 so abandoned (more than 3 years) is correct. The Doom9 archive (forum.doom9.org) returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the TNLMeans comparisons there are snippet-only and were not used for the tier.
